body:
Partners Group is rewriting the rulebook for several of its investment vehicles at once, responding to a shift in what clients want from their holdings. The Swiss private-markets manager is splitting one flagship, winding down another and building out a fresh income strategy — a three-front response to the same underlying problem: investors want their money back sooner than the old structures allowed.

At the heart of the shake-up is the Global Value SICAV, an evergreen private-equity vehicle with a net asset value of EUR 6.6 billion. Roughly two weeks ago, Partners Group set out plans to carve the portfolio into two sleeves with distinct investment and distribution profiles. One sleeve would keep reinvesting gains for long-term appreciation, while the other would return capital to investors through portfolio sales. Shareholder approval is still required before the umbrella structure takes effect.

The redesign followed a wave of redemption requests at evergreen funds, a trend Bloomberg has reported across older portfolios. Rather than force asset sales to meet withdrawals, the manager is trying to match its structures to the differing liquidity needs of its investor base.

Not every vehicle gets a restructuring. At Partners Group Private Equity Limited, holders opted for an outright exit. Roughly a week ago, 74.1% of shares voted in favour of the liquidity option, according to Reuters, shelving a previously planned reorganisation in favour of an orderly liquidation. At the extraordinary general meeting that followed, 99.89% of votes cast backed winding down the entire portfolio — and the sell-down began the moment the meeting closed. Capital tied up in the vehicle will now be released gradually as the underlying holdings are sold.

Though the trust is a standalone entity, the vote laid bare how sensitive institutional investors have become to liquidity promises.

Private Credit as the New Growth Engine

While it retools the existing range, Partners Group is pushing into higher-yielding territory. The firm launched a global multi-sector private credit income strategy, an open-ended evergreen vehicle aimed at institutional investors and private-wealth clients worldwide. It targets high single-digit to low double-digit returns, with income generated mainly through ongoing distributions. The portfolio is set to span direct lending, secondaries, fund financing, royalties and liquid credit.

If the income-oriented approach pulls in fresh capital, it could offset the standstill in private equity. The group is also still doing deals: the European Commission cleared its acquisition of AVK Power Solutions Limited, with the existing management team retaining a minority stake. Backers read that as a sign that selective bolt-ons and platform investments remain on track.

Jefferies Trims Its Numbers

The bear case rests on big allocators staying on the sidelines. Should the redemption troubles at evergreen funds fail to be contained quickly, organic growth could stall for years, with orderly wind-downs soaking up management capacity and sapping performance fees.

About two weeks ago, Jefferies cut its price target on Partners Group to CHF 605 from CHF 710 while keeping a "Hold" rating. The analysts trimmed their 2026 and 2027 earnings-per-share estimates by 10% and 11% respectively, pointing to the redemption issues at the evergreen funds. They see no meaningful recovery in assets under management before 2028. A persistently high interest-rate environment could also keep liquid alternatives looking more attractive than illiquid private-markets funds for some time.

The market has taken its toll. The stock closed Monday at EUR 639.40, down 40% since the start of the year, leaving it just 2.6% above its 52-week low. A separate reading put the price at EUR 649.40, down 39% year-to-date, and far below the 52-week high of EUR 1,187.50 — a gap that underlines the potential upside if sentiment turns.

The path forward hinges on clear operational tests. As long as the portfolio split runs smoothly and the private credit initiative delivers measurable net inflows, the shares may find a durable floor. Further liquidation votes or sustained redemption pressure at core vehicles, however, would likely trigger more estimate cuts and prolong the weakness in fee income.

The next hard data point is already circled: on 13 January 2027, Partners Group publishes its official assets-under-management figures for 31 December 2026 — the first clear read on how heavily the recent turbulence and restructuring have weighed on total capital.
